description: Python binding and companion gaps: PV sizing bindings, utils parsing, datetime parsing, metrics bindings, RL Gymnasium action mapping, HELICS time sync and signal mapping, and RL observation space.

reviews.title: Python PV sizing bindings: compute_usable_area, size_pv_system, enumerate_pv_candidates, infer_roof_shape, error propagation
reviews.prompt: The PV sizing Python bindings expose four Rust functions to Python: compute_usable_area(), size_pv_system(), enumerate_pv_candidates(), and infer_roof_shape(). Review each binding for correctness and error handling: (a) compute_usable_area: must accept roof geometry (area, tilt, azimuth) and shading obstructions, then return the net usable area for PV. Verify that the Rust implementation handles non-rectangular roof shapes, multiple roof faces, and partial shading (e.g., a dormer or chimney that shades part of a roof face). Check that the returned area is in consistent units (m²). (b) size_pv_system: given usable area, panel efficiency, and inverter specifications, compute the system DC and AC capacity. Verify that panel and inverter models are selectable (not hardcoded) and that the sizing respects electrical code constraints (e.g., NEC 120% rule for backfeed on busbar). (c) enumerate_pv_candidates: should return multiple PV system configurations with different panel/inverter combinations, system sizes, and orientations. Verify that the enumeration covers the search space comprehensively and that invalid combinations (panels that exceed roof area, inverters that can't handle the DC/AC ratio) are filtered out. (d) infer_roof_shape: given building dimensions and orientation, infer likely roof geometry (gable, hip, flat, shed). The inference should be based on the building footprint and a reasonable default for the climate zone (e.g., flat roofs common in Southwest, pitched roofs in Northeast). (e) Error propagation: Rust errors (invalid geometry, out-of-bounds values, numerical errors) must propagate to Python as descriptive exceptions, not as Rust panics that abort the Python process. Verify that every fallible function returns a PyResult and that error messages include enough context for a Python developer to diagnose the issue without reading Rust source. (f) Type conversion: numpy arrays passed from Python must be correctly converted to Rust ndarray types. Verify that the binding handles C-contiguous and Fortran-contiguous arrays, zero-length arrays, and NaN values.

reviews.title: Python utils parse_day_filter: all 9 filter strings, case insensitivity, error messages
reviews.prompt: The parse_day_filter function converts day-type filter strings to an internal representation used for scheduling (e.g., run equipment only on weekdays, or only during peak event days). Review the parser for completeness: (a) All 9 filter strings: verify that every valid filter string defined in the HARES specification is recognized. Common day-type filters include: 'all', 'weekdays', 'weekends', 'monday' through 'sunday', 'holidays', 'peak_events', 'non_peak_events', 'first_of_month', 'last_of_month'. If any are missing, those schedules silently default to 'all' (or worse, panic). (b) Case insensitivity: schedule strings may come from configuration files with inconsistent capitalization. Verify that 'WEEKDAYS', 'Weekdays', and 'weekdays' all parse to the same filter. (c) Combination filters: some scheduling systems support combined filters like 'weekdays+peak_events' (run on weekdays but only if it's also a peak event day). Verify whether parse_day_filter supports combinations and, if not, whether the documentation clearly states the limitation. (d) Error messages: when an unrecognized filter string is provided, the error message should list the valid options. A generic 'invalid filter' without listing valid values forces the user to read source code. (e) Return type: verify that the parsed filter type is usable by the scheduling engine without additional conversion. If parse_day_filter returns an opaque integer that must be matched to a meaning elsewhere, the abstraction is leaky. (f) Zero-length and whitespace-only strings: these should produce a clear error, not a default filter or a panic. (g) Unicode handling: filter strings may contain non-ASCII characters due to config file encoding issues. Verify the parser handles or rejects these gracefully.

reviews.title: Python utils parse_datetime_str: RFC3339, ISO 8601 T-separated, date-only, naive assumes UTC, DST consistency
reviews.prompt: The parse_datetime_str function (lines 28-50) converts datetime strings from Python configuration inputs to Rust datetime types. Datetime parsing is notoriously error-prone. Review: (a) RFC3339 format: '2024-01-15T14:30:00+05:00' should parse with the correct UTC offset applied. Verify that the offset is subtracted/added correctly and that the resulting UTC timestamp is right. A sign error in the offset calculation shifts timestamps by twice the offset. (b) ISO 8601 T-separated without timezone: '2024-01-15T14:30:00' (no offset) should be treated as UTC per the spec. Verify it's not treated as local time, which would shift timestamps by the machine's UTC offset. (c) Date-only: '2024-01-15' should parse as midnight UTC on that date. Verify the time component is set to 00:00:00 UTC, not 00:00:00 local. (d) Naive datetimes assume UTC: this is the documented behavior. Verify it's consistently applied across all parse paths. An inconsistent assumption (e.g., RFC3339 with offset becomes UTC, but date-only becomes local time) creates non-monotonic timestamp sequences. (e) DST transitions: if the parser uses a local-time-aware library and is given a datetime string that falls in a DST gap (spring-forward) or ambiguous period (fall-back), verify the behavior is well-defined. Prefer UTC parsing to avoid DST ambiguity entirely. (f) Leap seconds: '2016-12-31T23:59:60Z' is a valid RFC3339 timestamp (leap second). Verify the parser handles this gracefully (either by smearing or by rejecting with a clear error). (g) Sub-second precision: '2024-01-15T14:30:00.123456Z' should preserve microsecond or nanosecond precision. Verify no truncation to integer seconds. (h) Malformed strings: '2024/01/15', '15-01-2024', 'January 15 2024', empty string, garbage text—all should produce clear error messages, not panics or default values. (i) Year bounds: very old dates (before Unix epoch) or very far future dates should not cause integer overflow or panic.

reviews.title: Python metrics bindings: annual totals, monthly summaries, peak demand, LDCs, energy cost, unit consistency
reviews.prompt: The Python metrics bindings expose simulation result aggregation functions to Python users: annual totals, monthly summaries, peak demand, load duration curves, and energy cost. Review each metric for correctness and unit consistency: (a) Annual totals: verify that total energy consumption, total energy generation (PV export), net energy, total cost, and peak demand are computed correctly from per-timestep data. Check for off-by-one-timestep errors where the last timestep of the year is excluded. (b) Monthly summaries: verify the month boundary detection (especially for simulations that don't start on the 1st of a month or end on the last day). A simulation from Jan-15 to Dec-15 should not attribute December's second half to January. (c) Peak demand: verify this is the maximum demand over the demand window length (e.g., 15-minute or 60-minute rolling average), not the maximum instantaneous power. If the simulation timestep is 4 minutes, the demand calculation must average over the correct number of timesteps to match the demand window. (d) Load duration curves: verify these are computed by sorting all timestep loads from highest to lowest, then plotting against the percentage of time. Verify the x-axis is 0-100% of the period, not 0-timestep_count. (e) Energy cost: verify this matches the tariff calculator output exactly. Any discrepancy means the metrics layer is doing its own cost calculation rather than reading the tariff output. (f) Unit consistency: HARES internally uses SI units (Joules for energy, Watts for power). The metrics layer must convert to kWh and kW for reporting, as these are the standard utility and building-science units. Verify the conversion factor is 3.6e6 J/kWh (not 3.6e3 or 3.6e9). A wrong conversion factor makes all reported values wrong by a factor of 1000 or 0.001. (g) NaN and infinite values: if the simulation produced any NaN or infinite values (e.g., from a solver divergence), the metrics functions should propagate or flag these, not silently produce NaN outputs that downstream plotting tools display as blank. (h) Return types: verify that Python return types (dict, list, numpy array) are correctly typed and documented so that static analysis tools (mypy, pyright) don't flag them.

reviews.title: RL Gymnasium action mapping: PyNotImplementedError gap, what's needed for RL training completion
reviews.prompt: The RL Gymnasium integration currently raises PyNotImplementedError for action mapping, meaning no RL agent can actually send control actions to the simulation. Review the gap: (a) Current implementation: locate the PyNotImplementedError and document exactly which function(s) are stubbed. Determine whether it's the entire action space mapping or only specific action types. (b) Required action types: an RL agent controlling a residential building typically needs to set temperature setpoints (heating and cooling), battery charge/discharge power, EV charge rate, water heater setpoint, and optionally load shed commands for individual appliances. Each of these maps to a ControlSignal variant. (c) Action space definition: the Gymnasium action space (typically a Box or Discrete space) must map to valid ControlSignal parameter ranges. For continuous actions, the Box bounds must correspond to physically valid ranges (e.g., heating setpoint 15-25°C, battery power -5 to +5 kW). Verify that the action space definition in the Gym environment is consistent with the (unimplemented) action mapping. (d) Discretization: if the action space is continuous but the equipment accepts discrete commands (e.g., water heater on/off), the mapping must discretize the continuous action. Verify the discretization strategy (threshold, rounding, or stochastic) is documented and appropriate. (e) Invalid action handling: an RL agent exploring the action space will frequently send invalid actions (e.g., cooling setpoint above heating setpoint, battery discharge beyond SOC). The mapping must clip or reject invalid actions gracefully and return an appropriate penalty/reward, not panic or corrupt simulation state. (f) What remains: list the specific files and functions that need to be implemented to close this gap, the ControlSignal variants that need to be constructible from Gymnasium actions, and any dependencies (e.g., the control dispatch system must be fully wired before action mapping can be tested). (g) Integration test: once implemented, an integration test should run a random policy for 100 steps without panicking. The test should cover each action dimension at its minimum, maximum, and midpoint.

reviews.title: HELICS time sync: HARES timestep matching, end-of-simulation handshake, multi-rate co-simulation
reviews.prompt: HELICS time synchronization ensures HARES and external simulators (grid models, other buildings) advance in lockstep. Review the time sync implementation: (a) Timestep matching: HARES's simulation timestep must exactly match the HELICS federation's minimum time delta. If HARES uses a 4-minute timestep but the HELICS federation uses 5 minutes, the time sync will drift by 1 minute per step, accumulating to hours of mismatch over a day. Verify that the timestep is configured from a single source and validated at federation initialization. (b) End-of-simulation handshake: when HARES reaches its stop time, it must signal HELICS that it has completed and then finalize its HELICS connection. Verify that the simulation does not hang at the end waiting for a time grant that will never arrive, and that HARES properly unsubscribes from HELICS publications/subscriptions. (c) Multi-rate co-simulation: if external simulators operate at different rates (e.g., a grid model at 1-second timestep, HARES at 4-minute timestep), HARES must request time grants at its own rate while allowing the faster simulator to run sub-steps. Verify that HARES does not request time grants for every 1-second step (which would slow the federation to the fastest rate). (d) HELICS iteration mode: if the federation uses iterative time requests (where simulators can exchange data multiple times within a single timestep to converge), verify that HARES supports this mode or explicitly documents that it's single-pass only. (e) Error recovery: if an external simulator crashes or times out, verify that HARES detects the HELICS error state and shuts down gracefully rather than hanging indefinitely. (f) Logging: HELICS time sync events should be logged at appropriate detail levels—DEBUG for each time grant, INFO for period boundaries, WARN for sync anomalies. Verify the logging does not overwhelm the output when running a year-long simulation with 4-minute timesteps (131,400 steps).

reviews.title: HELICS signal mapping: bidirectional HARES ControlSignal ↔ HELICS signal, unit conversion at boundary
reviews.prompt: Every HARES ControlSignal must map bidirectionally to a HELICS signal for external co-simulation. Missing mappings mean external controllers cannot influence some equipment, or HARES state is invisible to external simulators. Review the signal mapping: (a) HARES → HELICS (publications): every measurable HARES state (zone temperatures, humidity, power draws, SOC, PV output, equipment status, control signal state) that an external simulator might need must be published. Verify that the publication includes units metadata so receivers can convert if needed. (b) HELICS → HARES (subscriptions): every HARES ControlSignal variant that an external controller might issue (setpoints, battery commands, load shed, DR signals) must be subscribable. Verify that incoming HELICS signals are validated (range checks, type checks) before being converted to ControlSignals. (c) Unit conversion at the boundary: HARES uses SI units internally; HELICS simulators may use various unit systems. Verify that unit conversion happens explicitly at the boundary, not implicitly in the mapping code. A power value arriving in kW that is interpreted as W creates a 1000× error. (d) Signal naming convention: HELICS uses hierarchical signal names (e.g., 'dwelling_1/zone_2/temperature'). Verify the naming convention is documented, consistent, and parseable. (e) Missing signal detection: if an external simulator subscribes to a HARES publication that doesn't exist, HELICS will produce a default value (typically 0). This can cause the external simulator to act on zero temperature or zero power, producing wrong results. Verify that all required publications are registered and that missing subscriptions are logged. (f) Data type compatibility: HELICS supports double, integer, string, boolean, complex, and vector types. Verify that the HARES signal type maps to the correct HELICS type and that automatic type conversion (e.g., a boolean status published as a 0.0/1.0 double) is intentional and documented. (g) End-to-end test: ideally, run a two-federation test with HARES and a simple external controller (e.g., a thermostat that reads temperature and sets a heating setpoint) and verify that the closed-loop behavior is correct.

reviews.title: RL observation space: state variables, physically correct bounds, no infinite ranges
reviews.prompt: The RL Gymnasium environment's observation space defines what state information the RL agent can perceive. The observation vector must cover all state variables relevant to control decisions, with physically correct bounds. Review the observation space: (a) State variable coverage: verify the observation includes outdoor air temperature, zone air temperature (per conditioned zone), zone relative humidity (or humidity ratio), electricity price (current and forecast), battery state of charge (%), PV power output (W), net load (W), time of day (sine/cosine encoding recommended for cyclic feature), day of week, and any DR event flags. Missing variables force the agent to make decisions with incomplete information. (b) Physical bounds: each observation variable must have finite, physically correct lower and upper bounds. Outdoor temperature: -50 to 55°C (not -inf to +inf). Zone temperature: 0 to 50°C. Relative humidity: 0 to 100%. Battery SOC: 0 to 100%. PV output: 0 to rated capacity. Electricity price: 0 to some reasonable ceiling (e.g., $1/kWh for critical peak pricing). Infinite bounds prevent normalization and cause RL training instability. (c) Normalization: the observation space should be normalized to approximately [0, 1] or [-1, 1] for neural network training. Verify that the normalization constants are documented and that the raw (unnormalized) observations are also accessible for debugging. (d) History/forecast: some RL algorithms benefit from a stack of recent observations or forecasts. Verify whether the observation space includes a temporal window (e.g., last 4 observations stacked) and whether forecasts (electricity price for next N hours, outdoor temp forecast) are included if available. (e) Zone count generalization: if the observation space is defined for a fixed number of zones, how does it handle dwellings with different zone counts? Padding with zeros vs. variable-length observation vs. separate environment per zone count. (f) Missing data at initialization: on the first timestep, some observations may not be available (e.g., battery SOC before the battery model has initialized). Verify the observation space provides sensible default values for the initial observation, not NaN or uninitialized memory. (g) Observation update timing: verify that the observation returned to the agent reflects the state after the previous action was applied, not before. An agent that makes a decision on stale observations learns incorrect dynamics.
